title: The Middle Years, 8 to 12
reflection: Think of a recent “that’s not fair” at home. What might my child have been trying to join to something they already hold?

questions.q: According to Lesson 5, what is a child of this age often doing when they say “That’s not fair” and keep asking why?
o: Passing a verdict on the parent, who has been judged unfair and must now explain.
Trying to join what was said to something held inside, and showing it in volume.
Dragging out the argument on purpose, to wear the parent down until the limit is lifted.
Repeating the arguments heard from other children, whose rules are not so strict.
questions.e: When a child says it, he is saying that what has been given has not yet met anything in him that makes sense of it. The “why” is the effort of joining, and at this age effort is often expressed in the only way a child has, which is volume. It is a message about a gap, not a verdict.
questions.c: “Why?” and “that’s not fair” as the effort of a mind joining what it is told to what it holds

questions.q: At eight o’clock a twelve-year-old protests that the screen limit is not fair, and lists the children who are allowed longer. Which reply fits Lesson 5?
o: Go through each rule in turn and defend it, until he can see that each one is sound.
Say she sees why it feels unfair, share her worry, and ask what he thinks it is.
Keep the line and end the talk, since explaining only invites the next argument.
Agree to a later time, so that he feels the rule is fair and drops the matter.
questions.e: Something like: “I can see why it feels unfair, because Mia gets longer at the weekend. Here is what I’m thinking about. What do you think I’m worried about?” A reason he works out himself lasts far longer than one he is handed. She may still keep the line, kindly and steadily; the aim is to give his mind the chance to settle.
questions.c: Bridge the gap with a reason the child can reach for himself

questions.q: An eleven-year-old, whose best friend would not let him sit at their table, says only, “It’s fine.” What should a grandparent do first, according to Lesson 5?
o: Fix it, by speaking to the friend or the friend’s family as soon as possible.
Tell him kindly that it will pass and that he is better off not minding it.
Explain that the friend is poor company and he is better off with others.
Name the feeling, and ask over some toast what he saw and how it felt.
questions.e: A child has only the felt sense, and the felt sense is hurt. The first gift is a little understanding: name the feeling, “that sounds lonely,” and then, when he is ready, ask what happened and what he felt. Friendships move because minds move, and it does not mean something is wrong with him.
questions.c: Name the feeling and ask; a child can respond and not only react

questions.q: A parent is worried about a friend her twelve-year-old has made. Which approach fits the picture of the fence round a young tree?
o: Forbid the friendship, since a young mind should be kept from company that may harm it.
Say nothing, since a child learns whom to trust only by making his own mistakes.
Explain her worry, keep sensible limits, and let the fence down as he understands.
Set a firm rule without the reasons, as reasons would only start a debate.
questions.e: While the mind is tender, rules are the fence, not a punishment, and they protect the young tree until it is strong. A fence is meant to come down. So the parent explains, and keeps explaining, and as the child understands he begins to choose for himself whom to spend time with.
questions.c: Rules are a fence that comes down as understanding grows

questions.q: “If a friendship between two children cools within a week, something must be wrong with one of the children.”
questions.e: When two minds resonate the feeling is of warmth and friendship. The mind is never still, so the same two boys can be very close on Monday and cool by Thursday, with no one at fault. A friendship cools as weather changes.
questions.c: Friendships move because minds move; no one need be at fault

questions.q: After missing a place on the school team, a twelve-year-old says, “I’m rubbish at everything.” Which reply fits Lesson 5?
o: “You’re not rubbish. You’re brilliant at lots of things, and that is what counts.”
“It is only a team, and it will matter very little by next month.”
“You wanted it and it hurts. That is a result, and it is not who you are.”
“Let’s write down all the things you do well, and read them through.”
questions.e: Take the disappointment seriously, and help him stand on firmer ground: “You wanted that place and you missed it, and it hurts. That is a result. It is not who you are. The one who wanted it so much, who tried and who feels this now, is still entirely here.”
questions.c: A result is not who the child is

questions.q: According to Lesson 5, where does a child’s lasting confidence rest?
o: In a good record of marks and results, built up steadily and patiently over the years.
In a steady supply of praise from the adults who know the child best and love him most.
In the child’s sense of doing at least as well as the other children of the same age.
In the truth of the child’s being, so praise and blame swing the mind less.
questions.e: Praise and blame will always come, and warm appreciation and honest feedback still have their place. But when a child is grounded in the truth of his being, they do not swing the pendulum of the mind so far. That steadiness is what we feel as confidence. The grounding comes first, and it is gentle.
questions.c: Confidence rests on the child’s inner ground, not on praise or marks

questions.q: “Since attention is the lens, hours of fast-changing screen time are a good way to build a child’s steady attention.”
questions.e: On a screen the scene changes every second or two, so the mind has almost no practice in holding on to anything. Its attention can grow scattered, and weak ripples leave weak impressions. The lesson says this without blame, and a scattered mind can be trained back.
questions.c: Learning needs attention held steady long enough, like the lens on the paper

questions.q: A parent whose seven-year-old is about to be given a phone asks what to do. Which approach fits Lesson 5?
o: Take screens away altogether, since a mind that is scattered cannot be trained back.
Give the mind something worth holding, such as building, drawing or a full story.
Allow short bursts of screen through the day, so that attention improves with use.
Offer a reward for each long stretch spent off the screen, until it becomes a habit.
questions.e: The answer is not simply “take it away.” Give the mind something worth holding: building, drawing, music, a story read in full, a long game, anything that lets the lens rest on one thing for a long time. And begin yourselves, because in the early years we learn more by doing than by understanding.
questions.c: Give the mind something worth holding, and begin yourselves

questions.q: A parent invites her child to sit quietly with her for three minutes, and the child does not want to join. Which response fits Lesson 5?
o: Insist on it every day for a week or two, so that the practice becomes a habit for him.
Drop the practice altogether, since a child who refuses will gain nothing from it at all.
Promise a small reward each time he sits, so that he comes to join more readily.
Sit anyway and leave the invitation open; the calm will bring him back.
questions.e: Invite your child to sit with you. Do not insist, and a child who does not want to join is not failing. The calm he feels will be what brings him back. Three minutes with no phone in sight is enough to begin with.
questions.c: Sit beside the child, a few quiet minutes at a time, without insisting
